sections.h2: Probate and selling an inherited Texas house
sections.html:
Probate is the court procedure that turns a death into a clear owner on paper. A buyer's title company wants that paper before it insures anything, so a Texas house tied to an estate generally waits on one of several routes before it can change hands.

Texas has no single statewide probate office. Each filing lands in a particular county, so the practical work is local even though the rules come from state law. The county clerk's office can tell you what it will accept.

Think of the process as three questions. Was there a will? Does the estate owe anything beyond a mortgage? Do all the heirs agree? The answers point to the route in the table below.

sections.h2: How long an heir can wait to offer a will
sections.html:
The usual limit is four years after the person dies, and the court may take a later application for an acceptable reason.

A signed will sitting in a drawer gives nobody authority over the house. If a relative died several years ago and nobody opened an estate, count the years first. A probate attorney, or the clerk of the probate court in the county of the person's last home, can say what the file shows.

  • A formal will is in writing, signed, and witnessed by two people.
  • A will in the maker's own handwriting needs no witnesses.
  • The application normally goes to the probate court for the county of the person's last residence.

sections.h2: Which probate routes fit a house?
sections.html:
The route depends on whether a will exists, what the estate owes and whether the heirs agree.

Routes to clear title on an estate house
RouteTypical situationPaper a buyer will see
Full administrationWill exists and a representative must collect assets and pay debtsCourt order, then an executor's or administrator's deed
Muniment of titleWill exists, nothing owed except real estate liens, no administration neededCourt order plus the will, filed with the clerk for the land's county
Small estate affidavitNo will, $75,000 or less in assets excluding homestead and exempt propertyCourt-approved affidavit; the homestead copy is recorded
Heirship affidavitFamily swears to who the heirs areSworn statement filed with the clerk
Transfer on death deedOwner signed and recorded one while aliveRecorded affidavit of death and death certificate

No route is quick by default. The best one is whichever the estate actually qualifies for.

sections.h2: When a muniment of title makes sense
sections.html:
It suits a family with a valid will, no creditors beyond liens on real estate, and no need for a personal representative to run the estate. The judge admits the will and issues an order, and both documents are filed in the land records of the house's county.

For a seller this is often the tidiest result, because a title company can read the recorded order and see who took the house under the will. A surprise debt from a credit card or medical bill can push the estate into full administration, so ask the family attorney to confirm that nothing else is owed.

sections.h2: Who can use a small estate affidavit?
sections.html:
Only estates with no will and no administration underway, assets under the $75,000 line (homestead and exempt property left out), enough assets to cover the debts and agreement among every heir. Estates Code chapter 205 sets these terms.

Two limits catch families off guard. The estate cannot hold land other than a homestead that passes to a spouse or minor children, and the court must approve the affidavit. Two disinterested witnesses swear to it, 30 days must pass after the death and no petition for a personal representative may be pending or granted.

  • A second house or rental lot usually rules this route out.
  • One heir who objects stops it.
  • Ask the clerk which forms the local court expects.

sections.h2: Heirship statements and transfer on death deeds
sections.html:
Either can sometimes stand in for probate, with a catch for each. The heirship statement is sworn and filed with the clerk without any judge reviewing it, and nothing obliges a buyer, lender or title company to rely on it.

The transfer on death deed is different because the owner prepared it before dying. It moves land outside probate, can be revoked by the owner and has to reach the land records before the owner dies. Afterward the heirs record an affidavit of death with the death certificate. The related Lady Bird deed, an enhanced life estate, lets the owner sell or mortgage without asking the people named to inherit.

When neither exists, the court options are a determination of heirship or an order of no administration.

sections.h2: Who signs the deed to the buyer?
sections.html:
The signer follows the route. A court-appointed executor or administrator signs after full administration. After a muniment, the heirs named in the will take title and sign. After a transfer on death deed, the beneficiary who recorded the affidavit signs as owner.

The clerk cannot add names to an older deed, so the proof of how title moved has to sit in the land records before the sale closes. The deed itself needs a notary or similar officer to witness the signature. Ask the clerk for the current recording charges, which follow a per-page schedule with local add-ons.

sections.h2: Property tax and the homestead exemption after a death
sections.html:
Property tax keeps running. Each year's tax lien arises at the start of the year, and the person who owned the house then is the one liable.

Texas ended its inheritance tax with Senate Bill 752, effective September 1, 2015. Heirs living in the house may keep claiming a homestead exemption. Heirs missing from a recorded deed hand the appraisal district a sworn ownership statement, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation. A spouse who is 55 or older may in some cases carry over the over-65 exemption. The appraisal district has the current forms.

sections.h2: What heirs should gather before calling a buyer
sections.html:
Gather the paper that proves authority, then list what the sale must pay off. Missing authority is the most common reason an inherited sale stalls.

  • The will, if one exists, and the date of death.
  • The case number from the probate court, or confirmation that none is open.
  • A search of the land records for a transfer on death deed.
  • Mortgage and tax balances, since both are settled from the proceeds.
  • A decision among heirs about who signs.

In order, the work usually runs like this: confirm whether a will exists, pick the route, get the court order or affidavit, record it with the county clerk, clear the tax and mortgage balances, then sign the deed at closing.

A title company can say what it needs before closing, and an attorney can confirm which route fits the estate. Once the order, affidavit or deed is on record, the house can sell like any other, and a cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender's appraisal or underwriting.

faqs.q: What is the time limit to probate a will in Texas?
faqs.a: Four years after the death, as a general rule. A court can accept an application filed later when the applicant explains the delay acceptably.

faqs.q: Can heirs sell an estate house before the court finishes?
faqs.a: Usually not to a buyer who needs title insurance. The buyer will want an executor's deed, muniment order or approved affidavit on record first.

faqs.q: What is the asset ceiling for a Texas small estate affidavit?
faqs.a: $75,000, with the homestead and exempt items left out of the count. The estate must also have no will, no open administration and unanimous heirs.

faqs.q: Is there a Texas inheritance tax today?
faqs.a: No. Senate Bill 752 repealed it as of September 1, 2015, though property tax stays due.

faqs.q: Which office records probate documents for a house?
faqs.a: The county clerk for the county holding the house. The clerk records the deed or order once it carries a proper signature and notarization.
